cards.body: Virus: hides inside a file and needs you to open it. Worm: spreads on its own across networks — no click required. Trojan: pretends to be legit software while smuggling in the bad stuff. Ransomware: locks your files and demands payment for the key.
cards.title: Malware: know the four horsemen

cards.body: Most successful attacks don't use genius zero-days — they exploit old, already-patched holes. Every update closes doors attackers were walking through. Turn on automatic updates for your OS, browser, and apps, and stop hitting 'remind me later'.
cards.title: Updates are armor, not annoyance

cards.body: The 3-2-1 backup rule: 3 copies of anything important, on 2 different kinds of storage (say, your laptop plus an external drive), with 1 copy offsite (cloud). Ransomware can't extort you if you can just wipe the machine and restore.

Spyware quietly watches what you type and where you go. Only install apps from official stores, check what permissions an app asks for, and if a free flashlight app wants your contacts — that's your answer.

choices: A virus needs you to open an infected file; a worm spreads on its own
A worm needs a click; a virus spreads automatically
They're the same thing
cards.explain: Viruses piggyback on files you open. Worms self-replicate across networks without any human action — which is why they can explode worldwide in hours.
cards.q: What's the difference between a virus and a worm?

choices: Ransomware
Spyware
Adware
questions.explain: Ransomware's whole business model is holding your data hostage. Offline backups make the threat toothless.
questions.q: Which malware encrypts your files and demands money?

choices: replicating itself across networks without human help
hiding in email attachments you open
pretending to be a system update
questions.explain: Self-replication is the worm's defining trait. Viruses need you to run an infected file; trojans need you to install them.

choices: Keeping software updated automatically
Buying the priciest antivirus
Never using email
questions.explain: Patching closes the known holes attackers actually use. Expensive antivirus on an unpatched system is a locked screen door.
questions.q: Best defense against most real-world attacks?

choices: Wipe the machine and restore from backup
Pay immediately to save time
Delete the encrypted files and move on
questions.explain: Backups exist for exactly this moment. Paying funds criminals and often doesn't even return your files.
questions.q: Your files are encrypted by ransomware and you have 3-2-1 backups. Best move?

choices: refuse and probably skip the app
allow it — games need that stuff
allow it, then revoke later maybe
questions.explain: Permissions should match the app's job. A game demanding contacts and mic is harvesting data, not entertaining you.
questions.q: A free game asks for access to your contacts and microphone. You should…

flashcards.back: Malware that encrypts your files and demands payment for the decryption key. Backups are the real defense.
Malware disguised as legitimate software. Named for the Trojan horse — the trick is the delivery.
3 copies of important data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite.
They patch vulnerabilities attackers actively exploit. Most breaches use known, already-fixed holes.

cards.body: A 16-character passphrase of four random words ('correct horse battery staple') is stronger than 'P@ssw0rd!' and actually memorable. The real rule: one unique password per site, because breaches leak passwords constantly and attackers try them everywhere.
cards.title: Length beats complexity — use passphrases

cards.body: Check the actual sender address, not the display name. Hover links to preview the real URL before clicking. Urgency ('act now or your account closes!') is the tell — legitimate companies don't threaten you by email. When in doubt, open the site yourself instead of clicking through.
cards.title: Spot phishing in ten seconds

cards.body: You get a text: 'Your package couldn't be delivered, confirm here: bit.ly/xyz.' That's smishing — phishing by text. The link leads to a fake login that harvests your credentials. Real couriers don't ask you to log in through a mystery link.

Use a password manager so 'unique password per site' is effortless — you only memorize one strong master passphrase. Then turn on two-factor authentication everywhere it matters: email first, then banking, then everything else.

choices: Ignore the link and log in via the bank's real site or app
Click fast — 24 hours isn't long
Reply asking if it's real
cards.explain: Urgency plus a link is the classic phishing formula. Never click through; navigate to the site yourself and check for alerts there.
cards.q: An email says your bank account will be closed in 24 hours unless you click a link. Best response?

choices: One breached site hands attackers the key to all your accounts
It makes passwords harder to remember
Websites charge extra for reused passwords
questions.explain: Credential stuffing — trying leaked passwords on other sites — is automated and constant. Unique passwords per site contain the damage.
questions.q: Why is reusing one password everywhere dangerous?

choices: An authenticator app (harder to intercept than SMS)
SMS codes (simplest, so best)
Answering a security question
questions.explain: SMS codes can be intercepted via SIM swapping. Authenticator apps generate codes on your device; hardware keys are even stronger.

choices: phishing — the domain isn't paypal.com
fine — the display name says PayPal
a new PayPal subdomain
questions.explain: Always read the actual domain. Attackers register lookalike domains (paypa1 with a one) precisely to fool quick glances.
questions.q: The sender shows 'PayPal Support' but the address is support@paypa1-secure.net. This is…

choices: Your email — it can reset everything else
Your streaming service
Your food delivery app
questions.explain: Email is the master key: password resets for nearly every other account flow through it. Lock it down first.
questions.q: What's the single most important account to protect with 2FA?

choices: length makes it hard to crack, words make it easy to remember
hackers can't spell
it contains no dictionary words
questions.explain: Every extra character multiplies cracking time. Four random words give ~50+ bits of entropy while staying human-memorable.
questions.q: A passphrase like 'tiger lamp rocket seven' works because…

flashcards.back: Four or more random words strung together. Long, strong, and memorable — better than short 'complex' passwords.
Manufactured urgency. 'Act now or else' is designed to stop you thinking before you click.
A second proof of identity beyond your password — a code from an app, a text, or a hardware key. Stops most account takeovers.
Phishing delivered by SMS text message — fake delivery notices and bank alerts with malicious links.

cards.body: Every scam runs the same three moves: contact out of nowhere, manufacture urgency or excitement, then demand payment in an irreversible way — gift cards, crypto, wire transfers. No legitimate organization takes gift cards as payment. Ever.
cards.title: The scam playbook never changes

cards.body: The pop-up screaming 'virus detected, call this number' is the scam itself — Microsoft, Apple, and Google never cold-call about your device. Real support waits for you to contact them. Close the tab, and if it won't close, force-quit the browser.
cards.title: 'Tech support' will never call you

cards.body: The padlock (HTTPS) means your connection to the site is encrypted — it says nothing about whether the site is honest. Scammers get free HTTPS certificates too. Judge a site by its domain and reputation, not the padlock.

On public Wi-Fi, assume someone could be watching. Don't log into banking or enter card numbers without a VPN — or just use your mobile data for anything sensitive. Turn off auto-join for open networks and forget them when you leave.

choices: a scam — tax agencies don't demand gift cards or threaten by phone
legit — better pay quickly
probably legit if they know your name
cards.explain: Government agencies send official mail and never demand gift cards, crypto, or instant phone payment. Hang up; look up the real number yourself if worried.
cards.q: A caller says they're from the CRA, you owe taxes, and you must pay with gift cards right now. This is…

choices: Overpayment scam — their payment will bounce, yours won't
A generous buyer
A bank error in your favor
questions.explain: The classic overpayment scam: the fake payment reverses days later, but the 'refund' you sent is gone for good.
questions.q: Someone overpays you for an item and asks you to refund the difference. What's happening?

choices: It encrypts your traffic so snoopers on the network can't read it
It makes the Wi-Fi faster
It hides you from the café owner legally
questions.explain: Open Wi-Fi broadcasts your traffic to anyone listening. A VPN wraps it in encryption between you and the VPN server.
questions.q: Why is a VPN useful on café Wi-Fi?

choices: No — HTTPS doesn't verify honesty, and the domain is fake
Yes — the padlock proves it's Amazon
Yes — deals sites are always fine
questions.explain: The padlock only encrypts. The misspelled domain is the giveaway — always type important URLs yourself or use bookmarks.
questions.q: A site has the padlock icon and the URL is amaz0n-deals.net. Safe to enter your card?

choices: Don't call — close it; Apple never does this
Call immediately before files are lost
Pay the small fee to unlock the computer
questions.explain: Fear plus a phone number equals tech-support scam. Real warnings never demand you call a number or pay on the spot.
questions.q: Your grandparent gets a pop-up: 'Call Apple Support now, your files will be deleted.' Best advice?

choices: Gift cards or crypto demanded under pressure
Credit card on a known store
Interac e-transfer to a friend
questions.explain: Scammers demand irreversible payments. Credit cards have fraud protection; gift cards and crypto are gone forever once sent.
questions.q: Which payment method should make you walk away?

flashcards.back: Always a scam. No real company or agency accepts gift cards as payment.
An encrypted connection — not a trustworthy site. Scammers use HTTPS too.
Fake virus warnings or cold calls demanding payment for 'repairs'. Real companies never cold-call you.
Treat it as watched. Use a VPN or mobile data for banking and logins; disable auto-join.
